title: Wet-Bulb vs Dry-Bulb vs Dew Point: Three Temperatures HVAC Engineers Confuse
h1: Wet-bulb, dry-bulb, dew point — three psychrometric temperatures
description: Cooling tower approach uses wet-bulb, not ambient. Sizing off dry-bulb oversizes chillers by 15–25%. Here is when to use which.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Dry-bulb reads air temperature. Wet-bulb reads evaporative-cooling limit. Dew point reads condensation onset. All three convert between °C and °F, but they are not interchangeable physical quantities.
body: A single ambient temperature reading answers none of the questions HVAC and data-center engineers actually need. Wet-bulb, dry-bulb and dew point each describe a different air condition, and each drives a different piece of equipment.

Dry-bulb: temperature a standard thermometer reads in still air. Wet-bulb: temperature a wetted-wick thermometer reads under airflow — bounded by evaporation. Dew point: temperature at which moisture in the air begins to condense.

In dry desert air, wet-bulb can be 20 °C below dry-bulb — evaporative cooling is highly effective. In humid tropics, all three converge to within 2 °C — cooling towers lose most of their advantage, direct chillers dominate.

A tower designed for 24 °C wet-bulb reaches ~29 °C water outlet with 5 °C approach. Same site's 35 °C dry-bulb would push the design to 40 °C outlet — 11 °C hotter — invalidating the process cooling loop.
Cooling towers and evaporative coolers: wet-bulb. Direct-expansion AC sizing: dry-bulb. Condensation risk and desiccant sizing: dew point.

faqs.a: No. Wet-bulb ≤ dry-bulb, always. The two are equal only at 100% relative humidity.
No — WBGT is a weighted composite (70% wet-bulb, 20% black-globe, 10% dry-bulb) used for heat-stress limits, not the same as psychrometric wet-bulb.
